definition: The language/action perspective "takes language as the primary dimension of human cooperative activity," applied not just in person-to-person direct (face-to-face) interactions, but also in the design of systems mediated by information and communication technology.
details: The perspective was developed in the joint authorship of Understanding Computers and Cognition by Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd in 1987.

explainer.lead: The language/action perspective treats language as the primary dimension of human cooperative activity and applies it to designing technology-mediated systems, not just face-to-face talk. It matters because it reframes system design around commitments made in communication.

tiers.eli5: It says that when people work together, what they say to each other — requests, promises, agreements — is the main thing, so software should be built around that.
tiers.practitioner: Designers apply it to systems mediated by information and communication technology, treating utterances as actions that create commitments. The pitfall is assuming conversational moves carry the same force across cultures and media.
tiers.paperLevel: A perspective that takes language as the primary dimension of human cooperative activity, applied to person-to-person direct interactions and to the design of systems mediated by information and communication technology; developed in Understanding Computers and Cognition by Fernando Flores and Terry Winograd (1987).

explainer.example: A workflow system is designed around requests and commitments exchanged between colleagues rather than around data records alone.
